question.text: Experimentally it was found that a metal oxide has formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi><mn>0.98</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">O</mi></math>. Metal M, is present as <math><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></math> and <math><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></math> in its oxide. Fraction of the metal which exists as <math><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">M</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>+</mo></mrow></msup></math> would be:

solution.text:
Consider one mole of the oxide, then

Moles of M = 0.98;     Moles of O2- = 1

Let 'x' moles of M are in +3 oxidation state, then Moles of M2+ = 0.98-x

On doing charge balancing we get 

(0.98 - x)2 + 3x  = 2

Or 1.96 - 2x + 3x - 2 = 0

Or x = 0.04

 ∴ %of M3+=0.040.98×100=4.08%
